_about: Short explanations shown when you tap ⓘ or a dotted-underlined term, and in Learn on the More tab. Keep entries to 2-4 sentences, plain English, and honest where evidence is weak. 'terms' are words in the app that link to the entry. 'link' is an optional page for more. Edit freely.

entries.title: Flow (cfs) and % of normal
entries.body: Flow is how much water is passing the gauge, in cubic feet per second (cfs). One cfs is about 28 litres a second. The raw number only means something compared with what's normal for that river on that date, which is why the app shows % of normal from decades of gauge records. Low water makes fish spooky and concentrated in deeper runs. High water pushes them to the soft edges.

entries.title: Upstream or downstream of the gauge
entries.body: The app finds your spot on the USGS river network and compares it with the gauge. Flow compared with normal usually carries along the same river, but a rise or drop takes time to travel: roughly 2-3 miles an hour, so the gauge can be hours ahead of or behind you. A tributary joining in between can change flow, temperature and color a lot. That's what 'Refine my spot with Claude' looks at. If you're on a different stream, set the flow from what you see.

entries.title: Reading the 7-day chart
entries.body: The solid line is the gauge's flow over the last week, and the dot is now. The shaded band is the normal range for today (the middle half of past years). Above the band is high water, below it is low. The dashed line is water temperature, when the gauge measures it. A line climbing steeply means a rise is under way. A line falling back toward the band after a peak is the 'dropping and clearing' window that often fishes best.

entries.title: Rising vs dropping water
entries.body: A river coming up after rain often fishes well briefly, as food gets washed loose, and then switches off as it muddies. A river that's dropping and clearing after a rise is classic prime time, especially for steelhead, salmon and streamer fishing.

entries.title: Water temperature
entries.body: Water temperature drives fish metabolism more than anything else. Trout feed best from the mid-40s to the mid-60s °F (about 7-18°C), with the sweet spot in the mid-50s to low 60s. Below 40°F (4°C) they're sluggish and want slow, deep flies. Steelhead and salmon have their own ranges: steelhead often chase swung flies best from about 40-55°F.

entries.title: The 68°F rule
entries.body: At about 68°F (20°C) water holds too little oxygen for a hooked trout to recover, so catch-and-release can quietly kill fish. Most agencies and guides stop fishing for trout at 68°F, fish only the cool early morning, or move to colder water. Some rivers have official 'hoot owl' closures in heat waves.

entries.title: Estimated water temp
entries.body: Many gauges don't measure temperature. The app then borrows a reading from the nearest gauge that does, or estimates it from the last few days of air temperature. Spring-fed rivers like the Au Sable stay cooler and steadier than the estimate suggests. A cheap stream thermometer beats any estimate: dip it in a few inches below the surface for 30 seconds.

entries.title: Water clarity
entries.body: In clear water fish see well and spook easily, so use longer, finer leaders and smaller, natural flies. A slight tint is often ideal: fish feel safe but can still find your fly. In stained or muddy water, go bigger, darker or brighter, and fish closer to the bank where the current is softer.

entries.title: Barometer
entries.body: Many anglers believe a falling barometer before a storm turns fish on, and a high, bright day after a cold front turns them off. Scientific evidence for pressure itself is weak. It's more likely the cloud, light and weather change that matter. The app only gives it a small nudge.

entries.title: Moon phase
entries.body: Fishing lore says the moon matters a lot, but a study of 361 freshwater trout trips found moon phase didn't predict catch rates. Where it can matter is at night: bright moonlight changes night feeding by big brown trout and affects mousing and the Hex hatch, which happen after dark. For day fishing, cloud cover and light levels matter far more.

entries.title: Light: dawn, dusk and cloud
entries.body: Low light (early, late or overcast) makes fish feel safer from predators, so they feed more boldly, chase streamers and take swung flies. Bright midday sun on clear water pushes fish deep and under cover: go smaller, deeper and stealthier.

entries.title: The conditions score
entries.body: A 0-100 estimate of how good fishing should be, built from water temperature, flow compared with normal, the flow trend, clarity, weather and light, hatch activity and, for steelhead and salmon, run timing. What you report seeing on the water adjusts it. It's a guide, not a promise: tap 'How this score works' to see each part.

entries.title: Run timing
entries.body: Steelhead and salmon live in the Great Lakes (or the ocean) and come up rivers to spawn at set times of year. If they're not in the river, the best rig in the world won't catch them. The app uses each river's typical run months, but runs shift with water temperature and rain, so recent shop reports are the best guide.

entries.title: Fresh vs dark salmon
entries.body: Fresh salmon just in from the lake are bright silver ('chrome'), strong and aggressive. The longer they're in the river, the darker they get as they prepare to spawn and die. Target fresh fish in runs and holes, and leave dark, spawning fish alone.

entries.title: Redds
entries.body: A redd is a nest of clean gravel where trout, salmon or steelhead lay eggs. Walking on redds crushes eggs. Look for light-colored, cleaned patches of gravel and step around them. It's good practice not to target fish actively spawning on redds.

entries.title: Skamania (summer-run) steelhead
entries.body: A strain of steelhead that runs rivers in summer rather than winter or spring. In Michigan the St. Joseph and Big Manistee get them. They're famously acrobatic and will often take flies near the surface in warmer water.

entries.title: Lake-run fish
entries.body: Fish that live in a Great Lake and run up rivers, like steelhead, salmon and lake-run browns. Dams block them, which is why many rivers have runs only below the first dam (e.g. Tippy Dam on the Manistee, Foote Dam on the Au Sable).

entries.title: Floating line
entries.body: The standard trout line. It floats, so you can mend it and see takes, and it suits dries, nymphs under an indicator and most streamer fishing in shallow water. 'Weight-forward' (WF) means the heavy part is at the front, which makes casting easier.

entries.title: Sink tips (T-8, T-11, T-14)
entries.body: A short section of fast-sinking line that gets swung flies down to the fish. The number is the grains (weight) per foot: T-8 is lighter and sinks slower, T-14 is heavier and sinks faster (roughly 6-9 inches a second). Use heavier tips in cold, deep or fast water, and lighter tips or a floating line as the water warms.

entries.title: Intermediate line
entries.body: A line that sinks slowly (about 1-2 inches a second). It keeps a streamer just under the surface, out of the wind chop, and is great for stripping flies in slow or shallow water.

entries.title: Polyleader
entries.body: A tapered leader with a sinking or floating core that loops onto your line. It's an easy way to fish a streamer or wet fly a little deeper without changing to a sinking line.

entries.title: Skagit and Scandi heads
entries.body: Short, heavy shooting heads for spey and switch rods. A Skagit head is built to cast heavy sink tips and big flies with little room behind you: the winter steelhead standard. A Scandi head is longer and more delicate, for floating lines, light tips and smaller flies. Both attach to a thin running line.

entries.title: Leader
entries.body: The clear, tapered link between the thick fly line and the thin tippet. The taper turns the fly over smoothly. Longer leaders (12 ft or more) suit spooky fish in clear, low water. Short leaders (3-6 ft) keep sinking lines and streamers deep.

entries.title: Tippet
entries.body: The final, thinnest section of line that your fly is tied to. You add new tippet as you change flies, so the leader lasts. Match its size to the fly: too heavy and small flies won't drift naturally, too light and you'll break off.

entries.title: Tippet sizes (0X-7X)
entries.body: Higher X means thinner and weaker. Roughly: 0X about 12-15 lb, 1X 10-13 lb, 2X 9-11 lb, 3X 7-8 lb, 4X 5-6 lb, 5X about 4-5 lb, 6X about 3 lb, 7X about 2 lb (strength varies by brand and material). Steelhead and salmon tippet is usually given in pounds instead (10-20 lb).

entries.title: The rule of 3
entries.body: A quick guide to tippet size: divide the hook size by 3. A size 18 fly suits 6X, and a size 12 suits 4X. Go one size heavier in stained water or for big fish, and one size lighter in very clear, low water.

entries.title: Fluorocarbon vs nylon
entries.body: Fluorocarbon sinks, is less visible underwater and resists abrasion: best for nymphs, streamers and anything subsurface. Nylon (mono) floats and stretches: better for dry flies. Maxima is a tough nylon brand popular for steelhead leaders.

entries.title: Tippet ring
entries.body: A tiny metal ring tied between leader and tippet. You then tie new tippet to the ring, which saves your leader from getting shorter every time you change flies. It's standard on euro rigs.

entries.title: Indicator
entries.body: A floating marker on your leader (a 'bobber'). It suspends nymphs at a set depth and shows takes: if it pauses, dips or twitches, set the hook. A good starting depth is about 1.5-2 times the water depth, deeper in fast water.

entries.title: Split shot
entries.body: Small weights pinched onto the leader to sink nymphs. Place them about 10-18 inches above the first fly, usually just above a knot so they can't slide. Add weight until your flies tick bottom now and then. Check local rules: some rivers limit or ban lead weights.

entries.title: Sighter
entries.body: A brightly colored section of line in a euro (tight-line) rig. You watch it instead of an indicator: any pause, twitch or sideways move means a take.

entries.title: Rod weight and length
entries.body: Rod 'weight' (3wt, 5wt, 8wt...) matches the line and the fish. 3-4wt suits small streams and light dries, 5wt is the all-round trout rod, 6-7wt suits streamers and big rivers, and 8-10wt suits steelhead and salmon. Longer rods (10 ft or more) help with mending, nymphing and swinging.

entries.title: Spey and switch rods
entries.body: Long two-handed rods (11-15 ft) cast with a sweeping 'spey cast' that needs almost no room behind you, which is ideal for swinging flies on big steelhead and salmon rivers. Switch rods (about 11 ft) can be cast with one or two hands.

entries.title: Euro (tight-line) nymphing
entries.body: Nymphing without a fly line or indicator: a long, light rod with a thin mono leader and a colored sighter, fishing heavy tungsten flies close to you. You lead the flies through the current while staying in direct contact, so you feel and see subtle takes. It's deadly in pocket water and riffles.

entries.title: Nymph fishing
entries.body: Most of a trout's diet is insects living underwater (nymphs and larvae). Nymph fishing drifts imitations along the bottom, under an indicator or on a tight line. It's the most consistent way to catch trout most days.

entries.title: Dead drift and mending
entries.body: Real insects drift at the speed of the current. A 'dead drift' means your fly does the same, with no line pulling it ('drag'). Mending is flipping the line upstream so the current doesn't drag the fly. Drag is the most common reason fish refuse a dry fly.

entries.title: Swinging flies
entries.body: Casting across and slightly downstream and letting the current sweep the fly across the river. It covers lots of water and triggers aggressive takes. It's the classic method for steelhead and salmon, and for soft hackles when caddis are hatching. Take a step or two downstream between casts.

entries.title: Dry-dropper
entries.body: A buoyant dry fly with a small nymph hanging below it on a short piece of tippet. You fish the surface and the subsurface at once, and the dry acts as your indicator. It's great in shallow to medium water in summer.

entries.title: Stripping streamers
entries.body: Pulling line in with your line hand to make a streamer dart like a baitfish. Vary speed and pauses until fish react. When a fish hits, set the hook with a sharp pull of the line (a 'strip-set'), not by lifting the rod.

entries.title: Dry flies
entries.body: Flies that float on the surface, imitating adult insects or terrestrials. They're the most exciting way to fish: you see the take. They work best when fish are rising to a hatch.

entries.title: Emergers
entries.body: Flies that imitate insects hatching, stuck in the surface film. When fish are rising but refusing your dry, they're often eating emergers just under the surface.

entries.title: Soft hackles
entries.body: Simple, sparse wet flies with soft feathers that pulse in the current, imitating emerging caddis and mayflies. They're usually swung down and across, and fish take hard as the fly rises at the end of the swing.

entries.title: Streamers
entries.body: Larger flies imitating baitfish, sculpins, leeches or crayfish. They target bigger, predatory trout and work best in low light, stained or rising water, and in fall. Woolly Buggers and Sculpzillas are classics.

entries.title: Egg patterns
entries.body: Imitations of fish eggs, such as yarn Glo Bugs or plastic beads. In fall, when salmon spawn, trout and steelhead gorge on drifting eggs, so egg patterns are deadly. Beads are often pegged on the line above a bare hook. Some rivers restrict beads, so check the regulations.

entries.title: Intruders and spey flies
entries.body: Large, long, flowing swing flies for steelhead and salmon. Intruders are built with a trailing hook and lots of movement, without much weight. Size and color follow water clarity: small and sparse when clear, big and dark or bright when stained.

entries.title: Skaters and waking flies
entries.body: Floating flies swung across the surface so they leave a 'V' wake. Summer steelhead in warmer, clear water will rise and smash them. It's a 'riffle hitch' when you add a half-hitch behind the hook eye to make a normal fly wake.

entries.title: Hook sizes (#)
entries.body: Fly sizes run backwards: a #20 is tiny (midges), a #14 is medium (caddis), and #6-2 are big (stoneflies, streamers). Odd sizes are rare. Match the size of the natural insect first, then its color.

entries.title: Tungsten beads
entries.body: Tungsten is much denser than brass, so a tungsten bead sinks a nymph fast without adding size. The bead size (2.5-4 mm) controls how quickly the fly gets down: bigger for fast or deep water.

entries.title: Attractor patterns
entries.body: Flies that don't imitate anything specific but look buggy and alive, like the Parachute Adams, Stimulator and Royal Wulff. They're a good bet when nothing obvious is hatching.

entries.title: Hatches
entries.body: A hatch is when aquatic insects emerge as winged adults, often in big numbers at predictable times of year and day. Fish key on them. 'Matching the hatch' means using a fly of the same size, shape and color. Michigan's famous Hex hatch happens at dusk in late June.

entries.title: Dropper off the hook bend
entries.body: The easiest way to fish two flies: tie a piece of tippet to the bend of the first fly's hook with a clinch knot, then tie the second fly to the other end. 16-24 inches is typical.

entries.title: Improved clinch knot
entries.body: The most common knot for tying a fly to tippet. 1) Thread the tippet through the hook eye. 2) Wrap the tag end around the main line 5-7 times. 3) Pass the tag back through the small loop by the eye, then through the big loop you just made. 4) Wet it, pull tight slowly and trim.

entries.title: Loop knot (non-slip / Rapala)
entries.body: Ties the fly with a small fixed loop, so streamers and swing flies can swing and dart more freely. 1) Tie an overhand knot in the tippet. 2) Pass the tag through the hook eye and back through the overhand knot. 3) Wrap the tag around the main line 3-5 times. 4) Pass it back through the overhand knot (the Rapala version adds one more pass through the wraps), wet it and pull tight. The linked animation shows the Rapala knot, a close cousin.

entries.title: Double surgeon's knot
entries.body: The quickest way to join two pieces of tippet or leader. Overlap the two lines, tie a simple overhand knot with both lines together, pass the ends through a second time, then wet it and pull all four ends tight.

entries.title: Blood knot
entries.body: A neat, strong knot for joining lines of similar thickness, like building a leader. Overlap the lines, wrap each tag around the other line 5 times in opposite directions, and pass both tags through the middle gap in opposite directions. Wet it and pull tight.

entries.title: Setting up an indicator rig
entries.body: From the top: fly line, then a 9 ft leader, the indicator set at 1.5-2 times the water depth, and split shot about 12-18 inches above the first fly (just above a knot). Then the heavier point fly, and a smaller dropper fly 16-20 inches beyond it. If you never tick bottom, add weight or move the indicator up.
